\title{Comment on "Discovery and Preliminary Characterization of a Third Interstellar Object: 3I/ATLAS" [arXiv:2507.02757]}

\author{Abraham Loeb}
\affiliation{Astronomy Department, Harvard University, 60 Garden
  St., Cambridge, MA 02138, USA}

\begin{abstract}
  The interstellar object 3I/ATLAS shows a weak cometary activity. Its
  brightness suggests a maximum radius of $\sim 10~{\rm
    km}~(A/0.05)^{-1/2}$ for an asteroid with an albedo $A$. I show
  that interstellar objects with that radius would amount to an
  interstellar mass density that is well above the expected mass
  budget of interstellar comets or asteroids. Given this budget, the
  detection rate of objects like 3I/ATLAS implies that it is a comet
  with a small core radius $<0.6~{\rm km}$, or a member of a rare
  population with a number density $\lesssim 5\times 10^{-8}~{\rm
    au^{-3}}$ for $R\gtrsim 10~{\rm km}$. The second possibility would
  suggest that the rare population of 3I/ATLAS objects favors plunging
  orbits towards the inner solar system to accommodate their inferred
  detection rate.
  
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

The interstellar object
3I/ATLAS\footnote{https://www.minorplanetcenter.net/mpec/K25/K25N12.html}
was discovered on July 1, 2025 with an orbital eccentricity of $\sim
6.1$, perihelion of $\sim 1.36~{\rm au}$ (expected on October 29,
2025), inclination of $\sim 175^\circ$, and a hyperbolic velocity of
$\sim 58~{\rm km~s^{-1}}$~\citep{Seligman}.

3I/ATLAS shows a weak cometary activity. Its measured absolute
magnitude $H_V=12.4$ implies an upper limit on its nuclear radius of
$R\sim 10~{\rm km}(A/0.05)^{-1/2}$, for an asteroid-like albedo, $A$.
The detection rate of its population, $\sim 0.2~{\rm yr}^{-1}$,
requires a local number density of interstellar objects bigger than
3I/ATLAS, $n_0\sim 3\times 10^{-4}~{\rm au}^{-3}$, assuming random
orbits outside the Solar system~\citep{Seligman}.

Here, I show that the combination of these two estimates leads to an
untenable mass density in interstellar objects, unless 3I/ATLAS is a
comet with a much smaller core ($<0.6~{\rm km}$) or an object with
radius $\sim 10~{\rm km}$ that favored a plunging orbit into the inner
solar system as a member of a population with a much lower number
density ($\lesssim 5\times 10^{-8}~{\rm au^{-3}}$).

\section{Mass Density of Interstellar Objects}

The Galactic mass density of interstellar objects similar or bigger than
3I/ATLAS is given by,
\begin{equation}
\rho_{\rm ATLAS}= n_0 \times \left({4\pi\over 3}R^3\right)\times \rho_{\rm s}~,
  \end{equation}
where $\rho_{\rm s}$ is the intrinsic mean mass density of objects of
radius $>R$. Adopting $R$ as the radius of the solid core of 3I/ATLAS
and using the fiducial values inferred by \citet{Seligman} for $R$ and
$n_0$, I get:
\begin{equation}
\rho_{\rm ATLAS}= 0.01~M_\odot~{\rm pc}^{-3} \left({n_0\over 5\times
  10^{-4}~{\rm au^{-3}}}\right)\left({R\over 10~{\rm
    km}}\right)^3\left({\rho_{\rm s}\over 1~{\rm g~cm^{-3}}}\right)~.
  \label{massd}
  \end{equation}

For comparison, the Galactic mass density for stars in the
neighborhood of the Sun is $\rho_\star \sim 0.04 M_\odot {\rm
  pc}^{-3}$~\citep{McKee}. The total mass density in heavy elements
that sources interstellar comets or asteroids is $\rho_Z \sim
0.02\rho_\star\sim 8\times 10^{-4}~M_\odot~{\rm
  pc}^{-3}$. Furthermore, it is reasonable to expect the mass density
of interstellar asteroids to be lower than the mass density of rocky
materials around stars. Adopting an ejection to interstellar space of
$\sim 10 M_\oplus$ in comets or asteroids per solar mass in
stars~\citep{Loeb}, yields the limit
\begin{equation}
  \rho_{\rm ATLAS}\lesssim 10^{-6}~M_\odot~{\rm pc^{-3}}~.
\label{Upper}
\end{equation}

The limit from equations~(\ref{massd}) and ~(\ref{Upper}) implies that
either $R<0.6~{\rm km}$ for $n_0\sim 3\times 10^{-4}~{\rm au^{-3}}$ or
$n_0<5\times 10^{-8}~{\rm au^{-3}}$ for $R\sim 10~{\rm km}$. In the
first case, the radius limit from equations~(\ref{massd}) and
(\ref{Upper}) is about twice the limit on the core radius of the
interstellar comet 2I/Borisov~\citep{Jewitt}.

\section{Conclusions}

I conclude that the Galactic mass reservoir in ejected rocky materials
from planetary systems implies that either: {\it (i)} the reflection
of sunlight by 3I/ATLAS originates from its cometary plume whereas
most of its mass is contained in a compact solid core with a radius
$R\lesssim 0.6~{\rm km}$; or {\it (ii)} 3I/ATLAS contains a solid
object with a radius of $R\sim 10~{\rm km}$ but the local number
density of interstellar objects bigger than its size is limited to
$n_0<5\times 10^{-8}~{\rm au^{-3}}$. Both of the above possibilities
ease the tension of not detecting many more interstellar objects with
smaller radii than 3I/ATLAS, as sub-km objects are expected to be much
more numerous than $\sim 10~{\rm km}$ objects based on their
statistics in the solar system~\citep{Broz}.

If 3I/ATLAS is a comet, then it will get brighter as it comes closer
to the Sun and its surface gets warmer. Upcoming data from
state-of-the-art telescopes, including the {\it Vera C. Rubin
  Observatory} and the {\it James Webb Space Telescope}, will be able
to better constrain the nucleus radius of 3I/ATLAS in the coming
months. If 3I/ATLAS is a solid object with a physical radius $R\gtrsim
10~{\rm km}$, then the limited interstellar reservoir of rocky
materials would suggest that its trajectory favored a plunging orbit
towards the inner Solar system, perhaps by technological design.

title: Predictive posteriors under hidden confounding
summary:
Predicting outcomes in external domains is challenging due to hidden
confounders that influence both predictors and outcomes, complicating
generalization under distribution shifts. Traditional methods often rely on
stringent assumptions or overly conservative regularization, compromising
estimation and predictive accuracy. Generative Invariance (GI) is a novel
framework that facilitates predictions in unseen domains without requiring
hyperparameter tuning or knowledge of specific distribution shifts. However,
the available frequentist version of GI does not always enable identification
and lacks uncertainty quantification for its predictions. This paper develops a
Bayesian formulation that extends GI with well-calibrated external predictions
and facilitates causal discovery. We present theoretical guarantees showing
that prior distributions assign asymptotic meaning to the number of distinct
datasets that could be observed. Simulations and an application case highlight
the remarkable empirical coverage behavior of our approach, nearly unchanged
when transitioning from low- to moderate-dimensional settings.

	\begin{abstract}
		
		Predicting outcomes in external domains is challenging due to hidden confounders that influence both predictors and outcomes, complicating generalization under distribution shifts. Traditional methods often rely on stringent assumptions or overly conservative regularization, compromising estimation and predictive accuracy. Generative Invariance (GI) is a novel framework that facilitates predictions in unseen domains without requiring hyperparameter tuning or knowledge of specific distribution shifts. However, the available frequentist version of GI does not always enable identification and lacks uncertainty quantification for its predictions. This paper develops a Bayesian formulation that extends GI with well-calibrated external predictions and facilitates causal discovery. We present theoretical guarantees showing that prior distributions assign asymptotic meaning to the number of distinct datasets that could be observed. Simulations and an application case highlight the remarkable empirical coverage behavior of our approach, nearly unchanged when transitioning from low- to moderate-dimensional settings.

	\section{Introduction}
	
	% Prediction in external domains is particularly challenging when hidden confounding influences both predictors and outcomes, complicating generalization under distribution shifts. Traditional methods, such as invariance-based approaches (REFSS) and worst-case optimization frameworks (REFS), often rely on stringent assumptions or over-conservative regularization that limit predictive accuracy.
	
	In recent years, there has been a surge of interest in machine learning methods that demonstrate robust performance even when there are shifts in the distribution between training and test data \citep{wong,shiftllms}. Much of the existing research in this area focuses on point predictions, %typically using squared error loss, % probabilistic predictions aim to provide a comprehensive measure of uncertainty regarding an outcome variable given certain covariates. Point predictions are 
    often necessary for %decision-making, 
	communication and traditional practices, requiring the definition of an appropriate loss function for evaluation, 
     typically squared error loss. In contrast, probabilistic predictions offer a detailed quantification of uncertainty for future outcomes and are typically more relevant for risk management and decision support purposes, though they are more complex to construct and communicate. %A key principle in this area is to maximize sharpness while ensuring calibration. Sharpness refers to how concentrated the predictive distribution is around a specific point, considered the most likely value. Calibration, on the other hand, ensures that the predictive distribution is statistically consistent with the observed outcomes, effectively linking predictions with actual results \citep{gneiting}.
	
	This paper focuses on creating probabilistic predictions for a response variable \( Y \in \mathbb{R} \) based on a set of covariates \( X \in \mathbb{R}^p \), %. A probabilistic prediction for \( Y \) is a probability distribution over \( \mathbb{R} \), which, unlike point predictions, fully captures the uncertainty about \( Y \) given \( X \). This approach not only provides point predictions for the mean and all quantiles but also 
     therefore yielding prediction intervals. When a machine learning strategy is trained on a labeled source dataset, it can be expected to perform well on an unlabeled target dataset drawn from the same distribution, provided that generalization guarantees hold \citep{lugosi}. However, numerous applications often experience distribution shifts, challenging the standard independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumption and complicating the use of existing prediction methods.
	
	The majority of research addressing distribution shifts has concentrated on point prediction in regression or classification. One notable strategy is {\em distributionally robust optimization}, introduced by \cite{sinha2020}, which involves minimax optimization over distributions within a certain distance or divergence from the observed data distribution. Another important approach, initiated by \cite{anchor}, employs a causality-inspired framework to leverage the underlying data structure, thereby improving prediction stability amidst distributional shifts. However, the regularization scheme proposed by the authors prevents the causal parameters from being the actual probability limit of the estimators they introduce; i.e., they are not asymptotically unbiased. 
	
	Another framework for quantifying uncertainty of any predictive algorithm is {\em conformal prediction}. Recent developments in this literature have shown a growing interest in robustness, particularly in constructing robust prediction intervals for a fixed marginal coverage level rather than estimating full distributions \citep{tibs19}. In addition, causality has recently been related to a certain risk minimization problem with a corresponding notion of robustness \citep{stspeter}. To our knowledge, only two studies address robust probabilistic prediction in the causality literature: \cite{kook} proposed {\em distributional anchor regression} for conditional transformation models as an extension of the above mentioned; and \cite{henzi} analysed invariance for probabilistic predictions penalizing empirical risk minimization with the variance of the scoring rule computed across environments.
	
	\cite{ai2024} argue that distribution shifts comprise both ``covariate'' and ``\( Y | X \)'' types of shifts.
	Covariate shifts refer to differences in the marginal distribution of \( X \) between training and target environments, due e.g. to age or gender distributional structure variations. \( Y | X \) shifts involve changes in the conditional relationship between the outcome and covariates, potentially due to unobserved confounders or noncompliance \citep{Robins1989}.
	\cite{ai2024} suggest reweighting training samples based on estimated covariate shift and adjusting confidence levels to accommodate the worst-case \( Y | X \) shift. Importantly, both types of shifts are fundamentally different: while covariate shifts can be identifiable from data, the type $Y | X$ itself is not inherently identifiable. 
    
    Work introduced in  \cite{meixide2025unsuperviseddomainadaptationhidden} formulates linear algebra hypotheses that enable identification of causal parameters through the so-called Generative Invariance (GI), a projection estimand that adapts predictions to unseen domains without requiring knowledge of the specific test distribution shifts or hyperparameter tuning. GI achieves identifiability under mild, verifiable conditions and accommodates the influence of unobserved confounders across heterogeneous training environments through a parametric component. By redefining the role of invariance and avoiding the over-conservatism of classical instrumental variable (IV) methods \citep{angrist1996}, GI ensures optimal predictions while preserving unbiased estimation of causal parameters, marking a fundamental shift from the traditional view of predictive robustness as a minimax optimization problem, as GI does not require introducing bias into estimators of causal parameters. This is made possible by a novel mechanism that overpasses regularization techniques typically used in robustness frameworks \citep{anchor,shen2025}. In this regard, GI is the first method exploiting distributional information from unlabeled data in the target domain to provide asymptotically unbiased domain adaptation. 
	
	This paper builds upon GI to enable further exploration and applicability of its core concepts bringing in Bayesian methods. Frequentist GI facilitates the derivation of an asymptotic normality result for causal parameters but does not say anything about uncertainty at the predictive scale on $Y$.  Here we shall provide principled uncertainty quantification for GI, which will be crucial in at least two important respects.
	

	
            First, we open the door towards credible intervals for causal relationships under hidden confounding and, therefore, enable simultaneous causal discovery and calibrated predictions in this setting: to the best of our knowledge, we deliver the first computationally feasible hypothesis test of a covariate being in the parental set of a target response in a linear structural equation model.
            Note that obtaining credible statements for existing causal discovery methods is often difficult as one would need to determine the distribution of causal effects estimators after having searched and estimated a graphical structure of the model. \cite{peters} were able to control against false positive causal selection gathering all submodels that are statistically invariant across environments in a suitable sense. Pursuing this thread further, \cite{fan2024environment} obtain a finite sample variable selection property and its asymptotic relaxation in high dimensions.  Two important limitations of this methodological family is having to assume no hidden confounding and the lack of computational scalability due to an exponentially increasing number of hypothesis tests to be performed, apart from being statistical power not well understood in their context. 
	
	Second, while classical definitions frame identifiability as a binary property (a parameter is either identified or not), we are the first to explicitly articulate the empirical manifestation of weak identifiability as a gradual phenomenon, intimately connected to ill-posedness of inverse problems, as extensively studied recently by \cite{ghassami2025debiasedillposedregression} and \cite{neweak}. In such settings—common in nonparametric IV models or proximal causal inference—the underlying parameter must solve a conditional moment restriction involving a compact or nearly singular integral operator. The inversion problem becomes ill-posed and—although the model remains formally identifiable—variance inflates, confidence intervals widen, and estimation becomes unstable. In our framework, this will manifest as the prior progressively taking control of the posterior as identifiability blows up.  As we will see, a posterior contracting toward the prior is reflecting violation of identification conditions revealing the regularized nature of Bayesian posteriors. This is in contrast to frequentist estimators, which exhibit exploding variances and numerical instability in the face of non-invertible or ill-conditioned design matrices. We make this transition from identifiability to non-identifiability visible and quantifiable, showing how Bayesian inference interpolates smoothly across this boundary. 
	
		We emphasize that IV should not be interpreted as an oracle for our method: IV is the causal truth when the goal is (asymptotically unbiased) estimation of causal parameters. However, for prediction we are rather interested in the whole conditional distribution of the response given the covariates. This includes the IV structural function plus the conditional mean of the residuals given the covariates. It is precisely this second component that \cite{meixide2025unsuperviseddomainadaptationhidden} successfully identified and incorporated in a principled manner, enabling an exact representation of the effect of hidden confounders on the response (when this underlying dependence is truly linear). 
	
Our method calibrates well even when prior information is not available: simulations have been performed using a frequentist ground truth— see Section \ref{sec:sim}, where it is clearly stated that the parameters in our simulated numerical experiments are deterministic. There is no substantive prior knowledge: aside from the empirical Bayes shrinkage on environment-specific covariate means we propose, the remaining distributions were chosen for technical convenience, following Bayesian ridge regression, and do not reflect genuine beliefs. The key message is that the prior is not used to incorporate subjective information—it simply absorbs the effects of poor identifiability. This is analogous to the well known example of Gaussian priors emerging as $l_2$ penalties in ridge regression: while not representing expert domain knowledge, they entail important technical consequences in terms of regularization.
	
	\subsection{Contributions and related work}
%	The contributions of this paper are therefore:

         We offer the first principled, unified, and practical solution to two longstanding and challenging problems simultaneously: conducting hypothesis testing for causal parenting and calibrating probabilistic predictions in the presence of hidden confounding.
      \cite{wu} introduce a hierarchical generative model that encodes the indices of invariant predictors as a latent Bernoulli vector and, then perform posterior inference—exact or variational—to identify features whose conditional relationship with the outcome remains stable across environments. Nonetheless, as \cite{wu}'s framework exploits the original invariance assumption in \cite{peters}—namely that the conditional distribution of the outcome given the truly invariant covariates is identical across environments—it inherits the same vulnerability: when hidden confounders induce violations of this assumption (e.g., the conditional model is misspecified because of omitting covariates), the method can still select non-causal features or discard causal ones. Likewise,  \cite{madaleno2025} reformulate Invariant Causal Prediction in a Bayesian setting—embedding per-environment coefficients in a hierarchical prior and using sparsity induced priors to screen for invariant parents—yet it still rests on the invariance assumption. \cite{holovchak2025} seek to recover interventional distributions, which are not designed for predictive purposes and do not provide built-in facilities for formal hypothesis testing. Our approach, on the other hand, supplies well-calibrated Bayesian posteriors for both causal coefficients and outcome predictions, yielding credible intervals and a causal discovery procedure that remain valid under hidden confounding with a shifted test environment. 
      
      We extensively evaluate the empirical coverage properties of our approach across a range of scenarios, varying both sample size (four levels) and covariate dimension (three levels). In all settings, the coverage achieved by our method closely matches the nominal theoretical level. In contrast, even the best-case performance of the baseline—Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)—is comparable to the worst-case performance of our approach.

	\section{Problem formulation}
	
	We use the basic setup introduced in \cite{meixide2025unsuperviseddomainadaptationhidden}
	to motivate the problem of interest.
	Consider analyzing the relationship between the random variables $X \in \mathbb{R}^p$ and $Y \in \mathbb{R}$, formulated 
	through the structural model
	\begin{equation} \label{scm_main}
		X \leftarrow (1-\theta)X_0 + \theta X_1 \textrm{ and } Y \leftarrow \beta^T_*X + \varepsilon_Y,
	\end{equation}
	where $\theta \in \{0,1\}$ is a binary indicator distinguishing between training ($\theta=1$) and testing ($\theta=0$) regimes. 
	$X_0$ and $X_1$ are independent $p$-dimensional random vectors. The error term $\varepsilon_Y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_Y|\theta] = 0$, but otherwise may exhibit dependence with $X_0$ or $X_1$. Upon conditioning on $\theta$, we relax the traditional independence assumptions between the components of $(X^1,\ldots,X^p)$ and $\varepsilon_Y$. This departure from conventional approaches accounts for potential hidden confounders, with the endogeneity between $X$ and $Y$ attributed to unobserved common causes impacting the 
 error term. Using training data $ {D}_1=\{ (X_{1,1},Y_{1,1}),\ldots,(X_{1,n},Y_{1,n})\}$, obtained when $\theta=1$, our primary objective is thus to develop predictions for a test set ${ D}_0=\{ X_{0,1},\ldots,X_{0,{n_0}} \}$, corresponding to $\theta=0$. Note that model (\ref{scm_main}) assumes only that the covariates distribution may differ between training and testing environments, without imposing any specific structure on the nature of this shift (e.g., additive), as is commonly assumed in the literature.

Following Theorem 3.2 in \cite{meixide2025unsuperviseddomainadaptationhidden}, the setup (1) enables frequentist identification of the causal parameter $\beta_*$ if $\mathbb{E}[X \mid \theta = 1 ] = \mathbb{E}[X_1 ] := \mu \neq 0$ in the one dimensional setting without requiring heterogeneous training sources,
     showing that the minimizer $(\beta_{opt}, K_{opt})$ of the population least squares risk 
    $$ (\beta,K) \longmapsto \mathbb{E}\left[(Y-\beta X-K(X-\mathbb{E} X))^2 \mid \theta = 1\right]$$ 
    exists, is unique and attained at $\left(\beta_*, \frac{K_*}{\operatorname{Var}X_0}\right)$ with $K_*:=\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_Y,X_0) = \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_Y,X_1) $ under model (\ref{scm_main}) and inner-product invariance conditions \citep{causaldan}. Therefore, the conditional expectation of $Y_0$ given $X_0$ becomes identified despite the presence of hidden confounders. A $p$-dimensional version of this identifiability result is provided in Theorem 3.4 therein, which states that if the population mean vectors of the covariate distributions corresponding to different data environments span $\mathbb{R}^p$, then $\beta_*$ and $K_*$ are identifiable.

	\subsection{Multiple predictors, multiple test environments}\label{sec:mul}
	
	Consider now the more complex case with $E$ training environments and $p$ covariates. Let $\mathbb{P}_e$, $e = 1, \ldots, E$, denote the law giving rise to each data source. The sample from the fully observed environments is, therefore,
    
		$$
		\left(X_{e,1}, Y_{e,1}\right), \ldots,\left(X_{e, n_e}, Y_{e, n_e}\right) \sim \mathbb{P}_e, \quad e=1, \ldots, E
	$$
		which we condensate through ${D}_E = \{(Z_1,X_1,Y_1), \ldots (Z_m,X_m,Y_m)\}$, where $Z_i$ is a dummy indicator denoting from which environment did the $i$-th observation come from and $m=n_1 + \ldots + n_E$. Recall the test sample is 	$
		\left(X_{0,1}, Y_{0,1}\right), \ldots,\left(X_{0, n_0}, Y_{0, n_0}\right) \sim \mathbb{P}_0
		$, from which just the covariates are observed and we want to predict the labels.  
	
	Assuming that the model coefficients are a priori normally distributed with mean zero and common variance, we arrive to a situation similar to a Bayesian version of the usual ridge regression procedure \citep{tew}, i.e., 
		\[
	\begin{aligned}
		&	Y_i \mid \left( X_i, Z_i, \text{parameters}\right) \sim N \left(\beta^T X_i + K^T (X_i - \mu^{Z_i}), \sigma_Y^2 \right),  \\
		&	X_i \mid (Z_i, \mu^1, \dots, \mu^E, \hat \Sigma_{Z_i} ) \sim N_p(\mu^{Z_i}, \hat \Sigma_{Z_i}), \quad i = 1, \dots, m \\
	\end{aligned}
	\]
where $\hat \Sigma_{Z_i}$ is estimated by computing 
 the covariance of the matrix %\texttt{cov(XZi)} 
    containing the covariate samples in the environment $Z_i$. 
    Note that an intercept is automatically included in the model by adding a column of $n$ ones to the design matrix $X$. In this case, if the predictors were originally in $\mathbb{R}^p$, now $\beta \in \mathbb{R}^{p+1}$ so that we need $Z \geq p+1$ data environments to identify $\beta$ and the new ingredient $K$. For instance, in a one-dimensional example, including an intercept just involves having to observe data from two different environments instead of one single dataset. There are no other constraints. Also, observe that the ``correction'' term has expectation $\mathbb{E}\left(K^T\left(X-\mu^Z\right) \mid Z\right)=K^T \mathbb{E}\left(\left(X-\mu^Z\right) \mid Z\right)=K^T\left(\mathbb{E}(X \mid Z)-\mu^Z\right)=K^T\left(\mu^Z-\mu^Z\right)=0$, so it does not have anything to do with the intercept. 
    
     The priors are specified as 
		\[
	\begin{aligned}
		\mu^1, \dots, \mu^E &\sim N_p(\hat{\mu}, {\Sigma_\mu}), \\
		\beta, K \mid \tau^2, \sigma_Y^2 &\sim N_p\left(0, \tau^2 \sigma_Y^2 I_p\right), \\
		\sigma_Y ^2 \sim \sigma_Y^{-2}  d\sigma_Y^2 &,\tau^2 \sim \pi(\tau^2) \, d\tau^2.
	\end{aligned}
	\]
		with $\Sigma_\mu$ built upon a correlation matrix $R$ with prior distribution $R \sim \text{LKJ}(2)$ \citep{lewandowski2009generating}, which has a single shape parameter $\eta$ so that the probability density function for a $p \times p$ matrix $R$ is $
\propto [\operatorname{det}({R})]^{\eta-1}
$, being the default prior assigned by Stan to correlation matrices. In addition, $ \sigma_Y^2$, $\beta$ and $K$ are independent conditional on $\tau^2$. When there is not strong prior knowledge about how much the regression coefficients should be shrunk, we can use a beta-prime distribution as a default prior for $\tau^2$, also known as the inverted-beta and Pearson Type VI distribution \citep{polson}, with density
	$$
	\pi\left(\tau^2\right)=\frac{\left(\tau^2\right)^{a-1}\left(1+\tau^2\right)^{-a-b}}{B(a, b)}, a>0, b>0,
	$$
	where $B(a,b)$ represents the beta function and $a=b=1/2$ is usually set, leading to the standard half-Cauchy prior. The latter is particularly useful as a weakly informative prior for scale parameters because of its heavy tails. 
	
We emphasize though that the specification of priors is not the central contribution of this work. In fact, it will be shown in Section \ref{sec:theo} that the prior affects the contraction rate only as a multiplicative constant, not through the exponential term.





	In the canonical Bayesian linear model, the posterior mode (and mean) is equivalent to the frequentist ridge estimate with penalty $\lambda=1 / \tau^2$. In our case, we shall express the population heterogeneity leading to each environment as sampled from a common prior distribution to get a beneficial shrinkage effect.  $N_p(\hat{\mu}, {\Sigma_\mu})$ is %not a subjective a priori distribution, but rather
     thus viewed as an empirical Bayes distribution characterizing the variability of the covariate means induced by naturally occurring environments.  It is useful to think of the first step of the data generating process as the covariate means being drawn from a common prior. Note though that we just plug the empirical mean and not the variance of this distribution, to avoid a problem
     frequently occurring in empirical Bayes estimation \citep{ritov}: for 
      simplicity, assume that $p=1$ and all the environments gave rise to the same number  $n$ of observations; then, it is possible to build, via maximum likelihood, an estimator for the Gaussian prior variance as $  \max \left\{\frac{1}{E} \sum_{e=1}^E\left(\hat{\mu}^e-\hat{\mu}\right)^2-\frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{n}, 0\right\}$
	where $\hat{\sigma}$ is a consistent estimator of an asymptotic variance. If the previous max collapses
     to 0, then the resulting posterior is a point mass and the empirical Bayes posterior predictive region is a singleton. We escape from this problem by associating a hyperprior to this parameter.

	We could derive the explicit expression for the conditional posterior distributions of $\beta$ and $K$ given ${D}_E$, as 
    we did in Section \ref{kkshawshank}, but it would not provide additional insights. Therefore the model is directly implemented in %the probabilistic programming software 
    \texttt{Rstan} \citep{guo2020package}. 
	For this, let us obtain the predictive distribution of $Y_0 $ conditional on $X_0$. \cite{meixide2025unsuperviseddomainadaptationhidden} show that we recover the test distribution under inner product invariance \citep{causaldan}, error Gaussianity and the so-called \textit{causal Mahalanobis conditions} as
			$$
	\begin{bmatrix}
		X_0 \\
		\beta^T_*X_0 + K_*^T \Sigma_0^{-1}\left(X_0-\mathbb{E} X_0\right)+\xi S_0
	\end{bmatrix} \sim \mathbb{P}_0
	$$
	with $S_0= \sqrt{\sigma_Y^2-K_*^T \Sigma_0^{-1} K_*}$ and $\xi \sim N(0,1)$ independent of $X_0$

    Denoting by $w = (\beta,K)$, the predictive distribution for $f = \mathbb{E}\left[Y_0 | X_0, w \right] = 	\beta^TX_0 + K^T \Sigma_0^{-1}\left(X_0-\mathbb{E} X_0\right)$ is given by averaging it with respect to the posterior as
	$$
	\begin{aligned}
		p\left(f \mid X_0, {D}_E\right) & =\int p\left(f \mid X_0, {w}\right) p({w} \mid {D}_E) d{w},
	\end{aligned}
	$$
	from which we obtain the predictive posterior by adding randomly sampled $N(0,S^2_0)$ noise. 
	
	An example of a case where the predictive posterior has a closed form expression is given by trivially pooling all the observations into one single training source (denoted by ${D}$) without considering the dataset indicators and assuming a fixed-design linear model $f = X^T_0 w$ with additive Gaussian noise $Y = f + \varepsilon_Y$,  $\varepsilon_Y \sim N(0,\sigma^2_Y)$. Then the posterior distribution of the conditional mean is $p\left(f \mid X_0, D\right) = N\left(\frac{1}{\sigma_Y^2} X_0^{\top} A^{-1} X^T Y, X_0^{\top} A^{-1} X_0\right) $ where $A=\sigma_Y^{-2} X^T X+\Sigma_p^{-1}$ and $\Sigma_p$ is the prior covariance matrix of $w$ \citep{rasmussen}. The posterior predictive distribution is $$p\left(Y_0 \mid X_0,D \right) = N\left(\frac{1}{\sigma_n^2} X_0^{\top} A^{-1} X^T Y, X_0^{\top} A^{-1} X_0 + \sigma^2_Y\right)$$ and we use it to build a credible interval $\hat{C}\left(\cdot\right)$ by considering, for instance, its $\frac{\alpha}{2}$ and $1 - \frac{\alpha}{2}$ quantiles.  In our more complex case, where $f$ and $\varepsilon_Y$ are not independent, even conditional on the parameters, sampling from the conditional predictive distribution $p\left(Y_0 \mid X_0,D_E \right) $ is just a matter of creating a \texttt{generated quantities} block in \texttt{Rstan} preceded by the likelihood and prior specifications discussed in this section and then sampling \texttt{normal\_rng(cond\_mean, sigmay);} where \texttt{cond\_mean} is $f$ and \texttt{sigmay} is $\sigma_Y$. 
    
    The computational and applied properties of our estimator will be explored in Sections \ref{sec:sim} and \ref{sec:quiron}. 
    Before, let us focus on an important consequence of Bayesian Generative Invariance (BGI).

	\section{Causal discovery under hidden confounding}\label{sec:sel}
	
	A type I error guarantee \citep{peters} for causal discovery is known to hold under the invariance hypothesis, which allows exploiting that the conditional distribution of the response given the complete set of corresponding direct causal predictors must remain identical under interventions on variables other than the target variable. However, the presence of hidden variables (the ``$Y|X$ shift'') breaks invariance. \cite{peters} obtain the intersection $\mathcal{\hat S}$ of all the subsets of covariates not rejecting the null hypothesis of invariance through a test able to control the proportion of false positive selections: $\mathbb{P}[\hat{\mathcal{S}} \subseteq \mathrm{pa}(Y)] \geq 1-\alpha $ where $ \mathrm{pa}(Y) = \{1\leq j \leq p: \beta^j_* \neq 0\}$ . Taking the intersection makes their  procedure conservative in terms of power, which, on another note, is highly dependent on the structure of the observed environments. 
	
	In turn, BGI is able to correctly estimate the posterior distribution of the causal parameters $\beta_*$ and $K_*$, and, therefore, automatically enables for hypothesis testing of one component $\beta^j_*$ being zero, $j = 1,...,p$. Since our method provides the posterior distribution $p(\beta^j_* | D_E)$ for each coefficient, we can construct a $(1-\alpha)$ credible region $\hat C_\alpha$ such that:
	$\mathbb{P}(\beta^j_* \in \hat  C_\alpha | D_E) = 1-\alpha$. 
		Given $\hat C_\alpha$, we can assess whether $\beta^j_* = 0$ is plausible by checking whether $0$ lies within $\hat C_\alpha$. 
	
	The solution we propose to this problem is also more natural because the invariance hypothesis- which, we emphasize, is not required in our approach- is always formulated based on the \textit{observed} environments $\mathcal{E}$: a subset of covariates $S \subset \{1,\ldots,p\}$ fulfills the null hypothesis $H_{0,S}(\mathcal{E})$- ``invariance''- iff  $\mathcal{L}\left(Y^e \mid X_S^e\right)$ (the conditional distribution of the response given the covariates in $S$) is the same for all $e \in \mathcal{E}$. This may seem a bit contradictory 
     as hypotheses should be assertions that hold or not pre-empirically, begging the following paradox: knowing which environments are observed or not turns out to be something known in the population world, prior to sampling-- what $\mathcal{E}$ is becomes an aspect of the underlying distribution before we even have sampled from it. We solve this issue automatically: given a sample $\beta^j_1, \ldots ,\beta^j_N$ from the posterior of $\beta^j_*$ we decide that $j$ is a causal parent of $Y$ when
	$$\begin{aligned} \min \left\{\left|\left\{i: \beta^j_{{i}}<0\right\}\right|,\left|\left\{i: \beta^j_{{i}}>0\right\}\right|\right\}<\alpha N, \end{aligned}$$
	interpreted as the posterior distribution being sufficiently shifted away from zero, either above or below.

	\section{Asymptotics}\label{sec:theo}
	
	This section develops the large sample theory for our proposed estimator. We begin by introducing the notation and generative model shared across environments, along with the assumptions necessary for the Bayesian framework. These components enable us to establish posterior consistency and derive exponential contraction rates for the posterior distribution over the shared parameters $(\beta, K)$. Notably, our results highlight two key phenomena often left unexplained by frequentist theory: robustness to near-violations of identifiability, and the role of natural variability across environments in shaping asymptotic behavior. We conclude with a discussion of asymptotic normality.
		
	Let \(D_{n,E}
		=\{(X_{ei},Y_{ei})\,:\,e=1,\dots,E,\;i=1,\dots,n\}\) be i.i.d.\ within each
		environment; to streamline notation, we assume the same sample size across environments, setting $n_e = n$ for each $e$. Recall we posited the following model for every environment \(e\), 
		\[ \begin{aligned}
		&Y_{ei}\mid X_{ei},w,\vartheta_e \;\sim\;
		\mathcal N\!\bigl(\beta^{\!\top}X_{ei}
		+K^{\!\top}\Sigma_e^{-1}(X_{ei}-\mu_e),
		\sigma_{Y,e}^2\bigr), \\
		&X_{ei}\mid\vartheta_e\;\sim\;\mathcal N_p(\mu_e,\Sigma_e)
		\end{aligned}
				\tag{M}
		\]
		where \(w=(\beta,K)\in\mathbb R^{2p + 1}\) is shared,
		while the nuisance \(\vartheta_e=(\mu_e,\Sigma_e,\sigma_{Y,e}^2)\) varies with \(e\). In addition, the theorems in this section require the following hypotheses.
		
		\begin{ass}[Coefficient invariance and underlying truth]\label{ass:truth}
			There exists a unique \(w^\star=(\beta_\star,K_\star)\) and environment-specific
			\(\vartheta_e^\star\) generating the data according to model \textnormal{(M)}
			for all \(e\).  
		\end{ass}
		
	 \noindent The crucial component in Assumption 1 is the identifiability of \(w^\star\), which follows from the linear independence
	condition on the environment covariate means in \cite{meixide2025unsuperviseddomainadaptationhidden}.
		
		\begin{ass}[Priors]\label{ass:prior}
			\emph{(i)} The prior \(p(w)\) is absolutely continuous and assigns positive mass
			to every neighbourhood of \(w^\star\).  
			\emph{(ii)}  Conditioned on \(w\), the nuisances
			\(\vartheta_1,\dots,\vartheta_E\) are \emph{a priori} independent with densities placing positive mass around each \(\vartheta_e^\star\).
		\end{ass}
		
		\begin{ass}[Finite KL variance]\label{ass:klvar}
			For every \(e\) and \(w\), the log–likelihood ratio per observation  
			\(\ell_{ei}(w)=\log\!\bigl\{p(Y_{ei},X_{ei}\mid w^\star,\vartheta_e^\star)/
			p(Y_{ei},X_{ei}\mid w,\vartheta_e^\star)\bigr\}\)
			satisfies \(\operatorname{Var}[\ell_{ei}(w)]<\infty\).
		\end{ass}
		
		\vspace{.3em}
		\noindent Denote \(k_e(w):=\mathbb E[\ell_{ei}(w)]\) the environment-wise gaps. Write the expected likelihood ratios as KL divergences and define $$k_{\min}:=
		\min_{w\neq w^{\star}}
		\frac1E\sum_{e=1}^{E}
		\mathrm{KL}\!\bigl(p_e(\cdot\mid w^{\star})
		\,\|\,p_e(\cdot\mid w)\bigr)$$
		
		% ------------------------------------------------------

		We start by establishing the posterior consistency of $(\beta,K)$, so that credible sets shrink to neighborhoods of $w^\star$ meaning that any posterior credible region of fixed nominal level will eventually cover only points arbitrarily close to $w^\star$. We recall that on general metric spaces, posterior consistency is equivalent to weak convergence of the posterior distribution to the Dirac measure at the true parameter value $w^\star$ \cite[Proposition 6.2]{ghosal2017fundamentals}. 
		
	
		\begin{thm}
			\label{thm:consistency}
			Let 	$\Pi_n(\cdot \mid D_{n,E})$ be the BGI posterior distribution. Under Assumptions \ref{ass:truth}–\ref{ass:klvar},  
		\[
		\Pi_n(\cdot \mid D_{n,E}) \rightsquigarrow \delta_{w^*}
		\quad \text{in } \mathbb{P}\text{-probability, as } n \to \infty,
		\]
		where $\rightsquigarrow$ denotes weak convergence of measures and $\delta_{w^*}$ is the Dirac measure at $w^*$.
		\end{thm}
		
	The posterior distribution is itself a random object because it depends on the observed data. Therefore, when we say that the posterior is consistent, we mean that it converges to a point mass at the true parameter value both in a measure-theoretic and probabilistic sense. Specifically, posterior consistency means weak convergence (outer convergence) of the posterior distribution to the Dirac measure at the true parameter $w^\star$, in probability (inner convergence) under the true data-generating distribution $\mathbb{P}$. The weak convergence describes the limiting behavior of the posterior as a probability measure, while the convergence in probability reflects the randomness induced by the data because the posterior itself is a random object. As a consequence of Theorem \ref{thm:consistency}, point estimates (e.g.\ the posterior mean or mode) are consistent: they converge in probability to $(\beta_\star,K_\star)$.
		
		In consonance with the theoretical properties in \cite{wu}, the next result entails that the posterior of $w$ contracts exponentially
		in $n$ and $E$, with a rate that improves under greater environment heterogeneity. Importantly, this is a phenomenon that the frequentist framework for causal robustness has not been able to satisfactorily account for \citep{shen2025}.
	
		\begin{thm}[Exponential posterior contraction rate]\label{thm:rate}
				Under Assumptions \ref{ass:truth}–\ref{ass:klvar}, 
			\[
			TV\!\bigl\{p(w\mid D_{n,E}),\delta_{w^\star}\bigr\}
			=\mathcal O_{\mathbb{P}}\bigl(
			e^{-\kappa\,k_{\min}\,nE}\bigr)
			\]
			
			\noindent for every $\kappa\in(0,1)$.
		\end{thm}
		
		
		
	
		
	\begin{remark}
		During the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:rate}, the impact of the prior pushing most probability into the neighbourhood of $w^{\star}$ has a scaling effect over the whole rate. This means that the influence of the prior is entirely outside the exponent involved in the contraction rate. 
		\end{remark}
		
		
		Finally, the well-known asymptotic properties of posterior distributions in Gaussian linear models  \citep{aos1,aos2} reveal that the posterior distribution of $w$ converges weakly to a normal distribution centered on $w^\star$. When the covariate dimension $p$ is fixed, this assertion can be established through the Bernstein-von Mises theorem because our specific problem satisfies the conditions for this theorem to hold by virtue of identifiability and well-definedness of the asymptotic covariance matrix of GI \citep{meixide2025unsuperviseddomainadaptationhidden} and because the priors over $\beta, K, \tau$ are absolutely continuous.

	\subsubsection{Multiple sources example}
	
	The data generation process in this example is designed to mimic scenarios where observed covariates \(X\) and the response \(Y\) are simultaneously influenced by unobserved confounders \(H\), and the relationships vary across different environments. 
	
	For each training environment \(e \in \{1, \dots, E\}\), we generate \(\lceil \frac{n}{E} \rceil \) observations of the response \(Y\) and covariates \(X\). The $q$ hidden confounders \(H \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times q}\) are drawn from a standard normal distribution \(H_{i, .} \sim N(0, I_q)\). The environment-specific component of the covariates  \(V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}\) is  generated from a multivariate normal distribution with mean vector specific to the environment \(z\) and a covariance matrix \(\Sigma_V\), so that $V_{i, .} \sim N(\mu_e, \Sigma_V)$,  $\Sigma_V = 0.5 \cdot ({1}_p {1}_p^\top) + 0.5 \cdot I_p$.
	
	The $p$ observed covariates \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}\) are generated as a linear combination of the hidden confounders and the environment-specific part $X_{i, .} = V_{i, .} + \Psi^\top H_{i, .} $, where \(\Psi \in \mathbb{R}^{q \times p}\) is a coefficient matrix encoding the influence of the hidden confounders on the covariates. The response \(Y \in \mathbb{R}^n\) is generated as a linear combination of the observed covariates \(X\), the hidden confounders \(H\), and random noise: $Y_i = \beta ^T X_{i, .}  +\phi ^T H_{i, .}  + \varepsilon'_{Y,i}$, where \(\beta \in \mathbb{R}^p\) is the %true 
      coefficient vector, \(\phi \in \mathbb{R}^q\) encodes the effect of the hidden confounders on the response, and \(\varepsilon'_{Y,i} \sim N(0, 1)\) is independent random noise.  The mean vectors for the environment-specific covariates %\(E\) 
        are systematically varied across environments. The mean vector of the covariates in each environment is given by $
\mu_j = \frac{2j}{p} - 1 + u_j, \quad \text{where } u_j \sim \text{Unif}(-1,1), \quad j = 1, \dots, p,
$ are drawn once per dataset (deterministic ground truth). 
	
	This process is repeated for \(E = p + 1\) environments to enable identifiability. A separate test dataset is generated using the fixed mean vector
$\mu^0_{j} =  \frac{2j}{p} +2 \cdot U, \quad \text{with } U \sim \text{Unif}([-1,1]^p)$,
and a perturbed covariance matrix
$
\Sigma^{0} = \Sigma_V + 0.5 \cdot I_p.
$

	\subsection{Case study: analysis of lifestyle factors affecting BMI} \label{sec:quiron}
	
	Consider analysing the causal relationship between lifestyle factors including alcohol consumption, smoking habits, sleep quality, and sleep duration (collectively denoted $X$), and BMI ($Y$) using a comprehensive proprietary dataset with individuals from various Spanish provinces. The dataset encompasses as well numerous potential confounding variables, including sex, cholesterol levels and glucose levels treated in our study for illustration purposes as hidden variables affecting both $X$ and $Y$ simultaneously. The province from which an observation originates serves as the dataset indicator $Z$.
	
	Our methodological framework applied to this case will rely on two key assumptions: first, we posit that the confounding structure remains consistent across different provinces (akin to the inner-product invariance assumption), implying that the distribution of hidden variables and their relationship with our variables of interest is geographically invariant; second, we assume the absence of direct causal paths from geographical location to BMI, ensuring that any influence of province on $Y$ must be mediated through $X$. This framework aligns with the structural equation model (1), with province serving as IV \citep{angrist1996}.
	
	The use of geographical location as an instrument finds precedent in the medical literature, with notable examples including \citep{beck2003, brooks2003, earle2001, hadley2003, leigh2004, mcclellan1994}. In our analysis, we designate Spanish coastal peninsular provinces as training environments and evaluate BMI predictions in Madrid, in the center of the country. While we benefit from access to true BMI values in the test domain for validation purposes, we acknowledge that such complete information is typically unavailable in real-world applications, where health researchers often just have access to covariate samples in test domains. Our analysis achieved a remarkable empirical coverage of $0.95$, with physical activity emerging as the sole causal variable using the selection criterion in Section \ref{sec:sel}.

	\section{Discussion}

We have introduced a new framework that delivers calibrated probabilistic predictions and credible causal discovery simultaneously, even when distribution shifts and hidden confounders undermine conventional methods. Unlike classical IV or minimax-robust approaches—which either sacrifice unbiasedness through regularization or offer no uncertainty quantification—BGI uses a hierarchical prior to fuse information from multiple training environments and unlabeled target data, yielding fully Bayesian posteriors for both causal parameters and future outcomes. We prove that these priors endow the model with rigorous asymptotic guarantees, turning the number of distinct datasets into a meaningful measure of precision, and show how BGI enables the first practical hypothesis test for causal parenthood under hidden confounding. Extensive simulations and a real medical case study confirm that BGI maintains almost nominal coverage from low to moderate dimensions, while ordinary least squares and classical IV fail to generalize.




Regression problems involving heterogeneous datasets with the same structure but originating from different sources—such as multiple countries, demographics, or experimental groups—pose challenges like varying data distributions, cultural biases, or contextual differences. For instance, predicting housing prices unbiasedly in a new territory could use our approach fed with estate data from different cities or nations, where local economic conditions or regulations introduce shifts in feature relationships. In clinical research, patient response data from different hospitals or trials may follow the same scheme but differ in underlying population characteristics. Our approach integrates these heterogeneous data sources in an optimal way; on top of this, its Bayesian character provides inference with well-calibrated uncertainty quantification, as our simulations show, and valid hypothesis testing.

 The interpretation of causal identification within the Bayesian framework remains an open and, to some extent, philosophical question. \cite{gustafson} argue that non-identifiability manifests as posterior flatness around causal parameters. Foundational work on Bayesian inference for the Local Average Treatment Effect \citep{imbensrubin} adopts what is known as the \textit{phenomenological Bayes} approach, which views sensitivity to prior specifications as a diagnostic tool for assessing which identifying assumptions can be reasonably imposed or relaxed in IV-like settings. In \textit{Robust Statistics}, \cite{huber2009robust} write: “Instead of worrying about things not under his control, the robust Bayesian is merely concerned with inaccuracies of specification.” \citep{wolpert2004berger} echoes this view: “In some sense, I believe that this is the fundamentally correct paradigm for statistics—admit that the prior (and model and utility) are inaccurately specified, and find the range of implied conclusions.” While this is a critical issue for the future of causal inference, the focus of this paper has been to develop a principled methodology that enables reliable prediction and uncertainty quantification in partially observed domains—without compromising the consistency of parameter estimation in the pursuit of robustness. This is essential to ensure the validity of the causal parenthood hypothesis test we introduce.
 
Classical Bayesian literature has long acknowledged the role of prior distributions in resolving identifiability issues, particularly in models where the likelihood is weakly informative or structurally deficient. For example, \cite{richgreene} developed a fully Bayesian treatment for mixture models with an unknown number of components, where identifiability is inherently limited by symmetry and label-switching. Their approach, using reversible jump MCMC, shows how prior structure—especially hierarchical priors—can regularize inference and enable coherent uncertainty quantification, even when classical estimators would be ill-posed or degenerate. Similarly, \cite{mullerrios} addressed the problem of designing efficient MCMC algorithms for inference with feedforward neural networks, where identifiability is lost due to the overparameterization and complex posterior geometry of non-linear architectures.  
 
 This perspective directly relates to the main  problem of our paper: the parameter $\mu$ (prior mean of the distribution naturally leading to the different covariate averages accross environments) enters into the model not as a nuisance to be estimated and fixed but as a random quantity. In the frequentist setting, lack of identifiability—e.g., when $\mu \to 0$—results in non-invertible design matrices and unstable estimators. We recall Figure \ref{violation}, where the posterior of $\beta$ shrinks towards its prior mean as identifiability deteriorates. While this introduces some dependence on the prior, it avoids the pathologies of the frequentist alternative. Again, this exemplifies how Bayesian methods can express the blurry nature of identifiability through the introduction of priors \citep{gustafson}.  The cost, of course, is that the results will depend to some degree on the chosen prior structure. 
 The adversarial machine learning (AML) arena \citep{cina2023wild} considers situations in which an adversary modifies the operational data distribution in pursue of some objective, thereby inducing a distribution shift. Bayesian approaches \citep{rios2023} seem natural to model the available partial information about how the attacker might have perturbed such adistribution. Moreover, as attackers interact with an ML system, they learn how to modify their attacks inducing further shifts. In this context, the {\em attacker} seeks to manipulate instances to fool an ML algorithm in search of one or more objectives depending on the application \citep{rios2023},	therefore inducing a distribution shift.

A natural extension of this work involves modeling adversarial attacks in machine learning scenarios where the attacker manipulates only the covariates with the goal of steering the posterior predictive mean toward a desired target value. Under a Bayesian linear regression model with a normal-inverse-gamma prior, this reduces to a constrained optimization problem in which the attacker perturbs the input data within a fixed $L_2$ norm budget to shift the predictive mean. The attack is feasible when the desired shift lies within a ball determined by the posterior mean of the regression coefficients, and the optimal perturbation aligns with the direction of those coefficients. If the attacker’s target is uncertain and modeled probabilistically, this uncertainty induces a distribution over the perturbations and, consequently, over the manipulated inputs. This distribution can then be used to update prior beliefs about the regression coefficients and other model parameters. A promising next step would be to extend this framework to BGI and investigate how such adversarial perturbations can inform or refine prior distributions in that setting.

    
	Another promising direction consists on relaxing the assumption that the distribution of confounders and their influence on observed variables remains constant across environments. Similar to our approach, where environment means are naturally sampled from a prior rather than relying on frequentist estimators, thereby easing strict frequentist identification conditions, each environment could be assigned a distinct $K^z_*$, all shrunk through a prior. More broadly, further investigation into relaxing identifiability conditions is needed and would have a significant impact on the field of causal representation learning, which currently relies on the assumption that the number of environments must at least equal the number of latent nodes \citep{jin}.
	
	Additional theoretical questions remain open for future investigation. First, when generalizing to a new domain we

	\section*{Appendix}
	\subsection*{Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:consistency}}
	

	Under model (M), the posterior density of \(w\) admits the representation
	\[
	p\bigl(w\mid D_{n,E}\bigr)
	=\frac{p(w)\,\exp\!\bigl\{-S_{n,E}(w)\bigr\}}
	{\sum_{w'}p(w')\,\exp\!\bigl\{-S_{n,E}(w')\bigr\}},
	\]
	where
	\[
	S_{n,E}(w)=\sum_{e=1}^E\sum_{i=1}^n
	\ell_{ei}(w)
	\quad\text{and}\quad
\ell_{ei}(w)
\;=\;
\log p_e\bigl(Y_{ei}\mid X_{ei},w^\star,\vartheta_e^\star\bigr)
-\log p_e\bigl(Y_{ei}\mid X_{ei},w,\vartheta_e^\star\bigr).
	\]
	By Assumption~\ref{ass:truth}–\ref{ass:klvar}, for each \(w\neq w^\star\)
	\(\mathbb{E}\bigl[\ell_{ei}(w)\bigr]=k_e(w)\ge0\) with strict inequality
	for some \(e\), and \(\ell_{ei}(w)\) has finite variance. We proceed following the same case analysis—branching into the regimes of increasing $n$ and increasing $E$—as in \cite{wu}.
	
	First, suppose \(n\to\infty\) with \(E\) fixed. Treating \(\{\,\sum_{e}\ell_{ei}(w)\}_{i=1}^n\) as an i.i.d.\ sequence with mean
	\(\sum_ek_e(w)=:E\,k(w)>0\) for \(w\neq w^\star\), the strong law of large numbers (SLLN) gives
	\[
	\frac{1}{n}S_{n,E}(w)\;\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}\;E k(w),
	\quad
	\frac{1}{n}S_{n,E}(w^\star)\;\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}\;0.
	\]
	Dividing numerator and denominator of the posterior at \(w^\star\) by
	\(p(w^\star)\exp\{-S_{n,E}(w^\star)\}\) yields
	\[
	p\bigl(w^\star\mid D_{n,E}\bigr)
	=\frac{1}
	{1+\displaystyle\sum_{w\neq w^\star}
		\frac{p(w)}{p(w^\star)}
		\exp\!\{\,S_{n,E}(w^\star)-S_{n,E}(w)\}}.
	\]
	Since for each \(w\neq w^\star\),
	\[
	\frac{1}{n}\bigl[S_{n,E}(w^\star)-S_{n,E}(w)\bigr]
	\;\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}\;-E\,k(w)<0,
	\]
	Lemma 2 of \cite{wu} gives
	\(\exp\{S_{n,E}(w^\star)-S_{n,E}(w)\}\to 0\) in probability,
	and hence \(p(w^\star\mid D_{n,E})\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}1\).
	
Second, suppose \(E\to\infty\) with \(n\) fixed. An entirely analogous argument applies by viewing
	\(\{\sum_{i}\ell_{ei}(w)\}_{e=1}^E\) as i.i.d.\ with mean \(n\,k(w)\),
	and again invoking SLLN and Lemma 2 of \cite{wu}.
	
	\medskip\noindent
	Consequently, since in either regime—\(n\to\infty\) or \(E\to\infty\)—we have
	\(p(w^\star\mid D_{n,E})\to1\) in probability, it follows that
	\(p(w^\star\mid D_{n,E})\xrightarrow{P}1\) whenever \(nE\to\infty\). \hfill $\square$

		
			\subsection*{Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:rate}}
			

				First, we look at the concentration of the KL sum. Recalling
				$S_{n,E}(w)=\sum_{e=1}^{E}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell_{ei}(w)$,
				with $\ell_{ei}(w)$ centred at
				$k_e(w)=\mathbb E[\ell_{ei}(w)]$,
				Assumption~\ref{ass:klvar} gives
				$\Lambda_{e}(\lambda,w):=
				\log\mathbb E\!\bigl[e^{\lambda(\ell_{ei}(w)-k_e(w))}\bigr]
				<\infty$, for $\lambda$ in a neighbourhood of $0$. The covariance structure is i.i.d. within each environment,
				so the usual Chernoff one–dimensional argument applies \citep{lugosi}: for every $t>0$
				\[
				\Pr \!\Bigl\{ \bigl|S_{n,E}(w)-\mathbb E S_{n,E}(w)\bigr|
				\ge t\Bigr\}
				\le 2\exp\!\Bigl( -\,\frac{t^2}{2nE\,V(w)}\Bigr),
				\tag{A}
				\]
				where
				\noindent $V(w):=\max_{e}\operatorname{Var}[\ell_{ei}(w)].$	Now fix $w\neq w^\star$ and choose $t=\tfrac12 nE\mu(w)$.
				Because $k_e(w)\ge k_{\min}$, inequality~(A) with
				$t=\tfrac12 nEk_{\min}$
				implies
				\[
				\Pr\!\Bigl\{ S_{n,E}(w)\le \tfrac12 nEk_{\min}\Bigr\}
				\le 2\exp\!\Bigl( -\,c_1\,nE\Bigr),
				\qquad c_1=\frac{k_{\min}^2}{8V_{\max}},
				\]
				where $V_{\max}:=\sup_{w}V(w)<\infty$ by Assumption~\ref{ass:klvar}.
				Then, with probability at least $1-\mathrm e^{-c_1nE}$,
				\[
				S_{n,E}(w)\;\ge\;\tfrac12 nEk_{\min},
				\qquad \forall\,w\neq w^\star.
				\tag{$\Omega$}
				\]
				
				Now we need to bound the posterior mass outside an $e^{-\kappa nE}$-ball. 
				Let $B_{r_n}=\{w:\|w-w^\star\|\le r_n\}$ with
				$r_n:=\mathrm e^{-\kappa k_{\min}nE}$ $(0<\kappa<1)$.
				Using standard arguments, we arrive to the following upper bound for the posterior tail outside the shrinking ball $B_{r_n}$				
				\[
				\Pi_{n,E}(B_{r_n}^c)
				\;=\;
				\frac{\int_{B_{r_n}^c}\!p(w)\exp\{-S_{n,E}(w)\}\,dw}
				{\int_{B_{r_0}}\!p(w)\exp\{-S_{n,E}(w)\}\,dw},
				\]
				where $r_0>0$ is small but fixed. 
				
				Let us provide now an upper bound of the numerator and a lower bound of the denominator. 
				On the event ($\Omega$) we have that $\displaystyle
				\int_{B_{r_n}^c}\!p(w)\exp\{-S_{n,E}(w)\}\,dw
				\;\le\;
				\exp\!\bigl\{-\tfrac12 nE k_{\min}\bigr\}\,P_{\max}\,\mathrm{Vol},
				$	where $P_{\max}$ bounds the prior density and
				$\mathrm{Vol}:=\mathrm{Vol}(B_{r_0})$ is the Lebesgue measure of the ball over which the integral in the denominator takes place. For $w\in B_{r_0}$, $|S_{n,E}(w)|\le c_2nE$ a.s.\ by continuity, so
				$\displaystyle
				\int_{B_{r_0}}\!p(w)\exp\{-S_{n,E}(w)\}\,dw
				\;\ge\;
				P_{\min}\,\mathrm{Vol}\,\exp\!\{-c_2nE\},
				$
				with $P_{\min}>0$ from Assumption~\ref{ass:prior}.
				
				Dividing both bounds gives the following non asymptotic probability bound:
				\[
				\Pi_{n,E}(B_{r_n}^c)
				\;\le\;
				\frac{P_{\max}}{P_{\min}}
				\,\exp\!\Bigl\{-(\textstyle\frac12 k_{\min}-c_2)nE\Bigr\}.
				\]
				
				\noindent where $P_{\max}:=\sup_{w\in B_{r_n}^c} p(w) $ is the maximum prior density outside the numerator ball and $P_{\min}:=\inf_{w\in B_{r_0}} p(w) = $ is the minimum prior density in a small ball around the invariant $w^{\star}$ involved in the denominator integral.

				Choose $c_2<\frac12 k_{\min}\kappa$ (possible by shrinking $r_0$) to obtain
				$\Pi_{n,E}(B_{r_n}^c)=\mathcal O_{\!P}\!\bigl(
				\exp\{-\kappa k_{\min}nE\}\bigr)$. Since the total variation between two measures is the infimum of their
				masses outside a common set,
				\[
				TV\!\bigl\{p(w\mid D_{n,E}),\delta_{w^\star}\bigr\}
				\;\le\;\Pi_{n,E}(B_{r_n}^c)
				=\mathcal O_{\!P}\!\bigl(
				\exp\{-\kappa k_{\min}nE\}\bigr),
				\]
				which is the desired rate. 	\hfill $\square$

\subsection{Single predictor, single test environment}
	
	According to \cite{meixide2025unsuperviseddomainadaptationhidden}, this setting enables frequentist identification of the causal parameter $\beta_*$ provided that $\mathbb{E}[X \mid \theta = 1 ] := \mu \neq 0$ without needing heterogeneous training sources, serving as a case for deriving theoretical insights while keeping the notation streamlined and accessible. We aim to 
	provide its Bayesian analysis to obtain the posterior predictive distribution required to issue the predictions.
	We have available  training data 
	${\cal D}_1 = \{ (X_1, Y_1),...,(X_{n},Y_{n})\}$ 
	and testing data 
	${\cal D}_0, = \{ X_{0,1},...,X_{0,n_0} \}$ , 
	with our objective being to predict the corresponding (missing) labels
	$\{ Y_{0,1},...,Y_{0,n_0} \}$ in this testing environment.
	
	\cite{meixide2025unsuperviseddomainadaptationhidden} show that the minimizer $(\beta_{opt}, K_{opt})$ of the population least squares risk $$\mathbb{E}\left[(Y-\beta X-K(X-\mathbb{E} X))^2 \mid \theta = 1\right]$$ exists and is unique and equal to $(\beta_*, \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_Y,X_0)}{\operatorname{Var}X_0})$ under model (\ref{scm_main}) and inner-product invariance \citep{causaldan}. Therefore the conditional expectation of $Y_0$ given $X_0$ becomes identified despite the presence of hidden confounders. 
	
	In the training environment, we formulate
	$$\begin{aligned}Y_i= \beta X_i +K ( X_i - \mu) + \varepsilon'_{Y,i}, \quad &\varepsilon'_{Y,i}\sim N (0, \sigma_Y ^2),  \\ 
		X_i \sim N (\mu , \sigma ^2 _X), \quad &i =1,\ldots ,n. \end{aligned}$$
	
	Let $\hat \mu = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$. We complete this with standard normal-inverse gamma priors 
	\citep{french2000statistical} from linear regression models
	as follows
	\[\begin{aligned} \mu | \sigma^2 _\mu \sim N(\hat \mu, \sigma_
		\mu^2),\quad &\beta, K | \sigma^2  \sim N(0, \tau^2\sigma_Y^2  ), \\  
		\sigma_{\mu} ^2 \sim \operatorname{Inv-Gamma} (a_\mu, b_\mu), \quad  &\sigma ^2_X \sim \operatorname{Inv-Gamma} (a_X,b_X) \\
		\sigma_Y ^2 \sim \operatorname{Inv-Gamma} (a_Y, b_Y), \quad &\tau ^2 \sim \operatorname{Inv-Gamma} (a, b) \end{aligned}\]
	
	The log-posterior may be calculated as 
	%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
	\begin{align*}
		&\log p(\beta, K, \mu,\sigma_\mu, \sigma_X, \sigma_Y, \tau | D_1) \propto \\ &\log p(Y|X,\beta,K,\mu,\sigma_Y) + \log p(X|\mu,\sigma_X) + \\
		& \log p(\beta|\sigma_Y,\tau) + \log p(K|\sigma_Y,\tau) + \log p(\mu) + \\
		& \log p(\sigma_X) + \log p(\sigma_Y) + \log p(\tau) \\
		&= -\frac{n}{2}\log \sigma_Y^2 - \frac{1}{2 \sigma_Y^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i - \beta X_i - K(X_i-\mu))^2 \\
		&-\frac{n}{2}\log\sigma_X^2 - \frac{1}{2\sigma_X^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i - \mu)^2 \\
		&-\frac{1}{2}\log( \sigma_Y^2\tau^2) - \frac{\beta^2}{2 \sigma_Y^2\tau^2} -\frac{1}{2}\log( \sigma_Y^2\tau^2) - \frac{K^2}{2 \sigma_Y^2\tau^2} \\
		&-\frac{1}{2}\log\sigma_\mu^2 - \frac{(\mu-\hat \mu)^2}{2\sigma_\mu^2} -(a_X+1)\log\sigma_X - \frac{b_X}{\sigma_X} \\
		&-(a_Y+1)\log \sigma_Y - \frac{  b_Y}{ \sigma_Y} 
		-(a_\tau+1)\log\tau - \frac{b_\tau}{\tau}
	\end{align*}
	Using standard arguments, the marginal posteriors for the variances are 
	inverse-gamma. In turn, observe that given $\mu$, the joint marginal 
	posterior of $\beta$ and $K$ is 
	$$\begin{aligned}
		&\log p(\beta, K \mid \mu, D_1) \propto -\frac{n}{2}\log \sigma_Y^2 
		- \frac{\beta^2}{2 \sigma_Y^2}  \left( \sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2 - \frac{1}{\tau^2} \right)
		\\&+ \frac{K^2}{2 \sigma_Y^2}  \left( \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \mu)^2 - \frac{1}{\tau^2} \right) 
		\\
		&- 2 \beta \left( \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i X_i \right)
		- 2 K \left( \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i (X_i - \mu) \right) \\
		&+ 2 \beta K \left( \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \mu) \right),
	\end{aligned}$$
	which corresponds to a bivariate normal distribution. 
	Finally, the marginal posterior of $\mu$ may be easily obtained by
	numerical integration.
	
	In the frequentist version of GI \citep{meixide2025unsuperviseddomainadaptationhidden}, if $\mu = 0$, the term $K(X_i-\mu)$ collapses to $K X_i$ making $\beta$ and $K$ unidentifiable since $Y_i = \beta X_i + K X_i$ could be satisfied by infinitely many combinations of that sum to the same total. 
	However, in the Bayesian case, we have additional information flowing through the model in two key ways. Because of the presence of the term $\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i - \mu)^2$, the model now captures the full joint distribution of $(X,Y)$, rather than just $Y|X$. 
	More subtly, the prior distributions on $\beta$ and $ K$ provide soft constraints on their values. Even when $\mu=0$, these priors make some combinations of  $\beta$ and $ K$ more likely than others, breaking the perfect symmetry that causes the identifiability issue in the frequentist case, see \citep{richgreene,mullerrios} for 
	related discussions. 
	Predictive distributions are described in the more general setting at the end of the nex Section.

title: Proceedings of the 19th International Workshop on Logical and Semantic Frameworks, with Applications
summary:
This volume contains the post-proceedings of the 19th LSFA, which was held in
Goi\^ania, the capital of Goi\'as state in Brazil, from September 18 to
September 20, 2024.
  Logical and semantic frameworks are formal languages used to represent
logics, languages and systems. These frameworks provide foundations for the
formal specification of systems and programming languages, supporting tool
development and reasoning.
  The aim of this series is bringing together theoreticians and practitioners
to promote new techniques and results, from the theoretical side, and feedback
on the implementation and use of such techniques and results, from the
practical side. LSFA includes areas such as proof and type theory, equational
deduction and rewriting systems, automated reasoning and concurrency theory.

title: Modeling of Vertical Distribution of Suspended Sediment Concentration in Open Channel Turbulent Flows Using Fractional Differential Entropy
summary:
Suspended sediment concentration and sediment transport heavily correlates to
fluid behavior, thus proving it to be a lucrative field for exploration. Most
of the existing deterministic and probabilistic methods proved to be complex
with high computation cost. In this paper, we proposed a simpler yet accurate
and cost effective concentration model using fractional entropy due to Ubriaco
for continuous domain, termed as fractional differential entropy (FDE). We
estimated the type I distribution of suspended sediment concentration along the
vertical direction in open channels considering the dimensionless normalized
concentration as a random variable and constructing an optimization problem
using the FDE. The surface concentration is assumed to be zero throughout the
study. We further validate our FDE based concentration distribution model
through regression and error analysis using some selected experimental and
field data. The results are compared with the existing concentration models,
which show the superiority of the proposed model with respect to the aspects
considered under this study.

title: Large Language Models Predict Human Well-being -- But Not Equally Everywhere
summary:
Subjective well-being is a key metric in economic, medical, and policy
decision-making. As artificial intelligence provides scalable tools for
modelling human outcomes, it is crucial to evaluate whether large language
models (LLMs) can accurately predict well-being across diverse global
populations. We evaluate four leading LLMs using data from 64,000 individuals
in 64 countries. While LLMs capture broad correlates such as income and health,
their predictive accuracy decreases in countries underrepresented in the
training data, highlighting systematic biases rooted in global digital and
economic inequality. A pre-registered experiment demonstrates that LLMs rely on
surface-level linguistic similarity rather than conceptual understanding,
leading to systematic misestimations in unfamiliar or resource-limited
settings. Injecting findings from underrepresented contexts substantially
enhances performance, but a significant gap remains. These results highlight
both the promise and limitations of LLMs in predicting global well-being,
underscoring the importance of robust validation prior to their implementation
across these areas.

title: Measure equivalence and sofic approximations
summary:
We introduce a technique for producing a measure coupling between two sofic
groups from a family of maps between their sofic approximations. We exploit
this to construct measure couplings between pairs of groups with prescribed
integrability conditions. As an application we show that solvable
Baumslag-Solitar groups, Lamplighters and the group SOL are all exponentially
measure equivalent to one another: in particular they are L^p measure
equivalent for all p. This is in sharp contrast with the fact that these groups
are in general not quasi-isometric to one another: indeed, for instance the
lamplighter with lamp group Z/3Z is not quasi-isometric the lamplighter with
lamp group Z/2Z.

title: Off-diagonal deformations of regular Schwarzschild black holes and general relativistic G. Perelman thermodynamics
summary:
We construct new classes of solutions describing generic off-diagonal
deformations of regular Schwarzschild black holes (BHs) in general relativity
(GR). Examples of such (primary) diagonal metrics reducing the Einstein
equations to integrable systems of nonlinear ordinary differential equations
were studied in a recent work by R. Casadio, A. Kamenshchik and J. Ovalle in
Phys. Rev. D 111 (2025) 064036. We develop and apply our anholonomic frame and
connection deformations method, which allows us to generate new classes of
target off-diagonal solutions. Ansatz that reduces the gravitational field
equations to systems of (exactly or parametric) integrable systems of nonlinear
partial differential equations are used. We find and analyze certain families
of deformed regular BHs containing an off-diagonal de Sitter condensate
encoding solitonic vacuum configurations, with possible deformations of
horizons and/or gravitational polarizations of constants. We emphasize that
general off-diagonal solutions do not involve certain hypersurface or
holographic configurations. This means that the Bekenstein-Hawking
thermodynamic paradigm is not applicable for characterizing the physical
properties of such target regular solutions. We argue that the concept of G.
Perelman's entropy and relativistic geometric flow thermodynamics is more
appropriate. Using nonlinear symmetries involving effective cosmological
constants, we show how to compute thermodynamic variables for various classes
of physically essential solutions in GR.

title: Blackbody radiation Zeeman shift in Rydberg atoms
summary:
We consider the Zeeman shift in Rydberg atoms induced by room-temperature
blackbody radiation (BBR). BBR shifts to the Rydberg levels are dominated by
the familiar BBR Stark shift. However, the BBR Stark shift and the BBR Zeeman
shift exhibit different behaviors with respect to the principal quantum number
of the Rydberg electron. Namely, the BBR Stark shift asymptotically approaches
a constant value given by a universal expression, whereas the BBR Zeeman shift
grows steeply with principal quantum number due to the diamagnetic
contribution. We show that for transitions between Rydberg states, where only
the differential shift between levels is of concern, the BBR Zeeman shift can
surpass the BBR Stark shift. We exemplify this in the context of a proposed
experiment targeting a precise determination of the Rydberg constant.

title: Building a monostable tetrahedron
summary:
In this short note we describe what we believe to be the first working model
of a monostable tetrahedron.

title: Multiscale Geodesic Flows
summary:
A system of equations for Multiscale Geodesic Flow (MGF) is introduced whose
solutions illustrate the paradigm of whorls within whorls within whorls,
introduced by L. F. Richardson in 1922 to describe the cascade of energy in
fluid turbulence. Numerical simulations are given for MGF on $S^1$.

title: Probability-Raising Causality for Uncertain Parametric Markov Decision Processes with PAC Guarantees
summary:
Recent decision-making systems are increasingly complicated, making it
crucial to verify and understand their behavior for a given specification. A
promising approach is to comprehensively explain undesired behavior in the
systems modeled by Markov decision processes (MDPs) through formal verification
and causal reasoning. However, the reliable explanation using model-based
probabilistic causal analysis has not been explored when the MDP's transition
probabilities are uncertain. This paper proposes a method to identify potential
causes of undesired behaviors in an uncertain parametric MDP (upMDP) using
parameter sampling, model checking, and a set covering for the samples. A cause
is defined as a subset of states based on a probability-raising principle. We
show that the probability of each identified subset being a cause exceeds a
specified threshold. Further, a lower bound of the probability that the
undesired paths visit the subsets is maximized as much as possible while
satisfying a nonredundancy condition. While computing these probabilities is
complicated, this study derives probabilistically approximately correct lower
bounds of both probabilities by the sampling. We demonstrate the effectiveness
of the proposed method through a path-planning scenario.

title: Prospective Learning in Retrospect
summary:
In most real-world applications of artificial intelligence, the distributions
of the data and the goals of the learners tend to change over time. The
Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning framework, which underpins most
machine learning algorithms, fails to account for dynamic data distributions
and evolving objectives, often resulting in suboptimal performance. Prospective
learning is a recently introduced mathematical framework that overcomes some of
these limitations. We build on this framework to present preliminary results
that improve the algorithm and numerical results, and extend prospective
learning to sequential decision-making scenarios, specifically foraging. Code
is available at: https://github.com/neurodata/prolearn2.

bib.abstract:
The two fields of machine learning and graphical causality arose
and developed separately. However, there is now cross-pollination
and increasing interest in both fields to benefit from the
advances of the other. In the present paper, we review
fundamental concepts of causal inference and relate them to
crucial open problems of machine learning, including transfer and
generalization, thereby assaying how causality can contribute to
modern machine learning research. This also applies in the
opposite direction: we note that most work in causality starts
from the premise that the causal variables are given. A central
problem for AI and causality is, thus, causal representation
learning, the discovery of high-level causal variables from
low-level observations. Finally, we delineate some implications
of causality for machine learning and propose key research areas
at the intersection of both communities.

bib.abstract:
Deep neural networks (`deep learning') have emerged as a
technology of choice to tackle problems in speech recognition,
computer vision, finance, etc. However, adoption of deep
learning in physical domains brings substantial challenges
stemming from the correlative nature of deep learning methods
compared to the causal, hypothesis driven nature of modern
science. We argue that the broad adoption of Bayesian methods
incorporating prior knowledge, development of solutions with
incorporated physical constraints and parsimonious structural
descriptors and generative models, and ultimately adoption of
causal models, offers a path forward for fundamental and applied
research.

bib.abstract:
Graphical causal inference as pioneered by Judea Pearl arose from
research on artificial intelligence (AI), and for a long time had
little connection to the field of machine learning. This article
discusses where links have been and should be established,
introducing key concepts along the way. It argues that the hard
open problems of machine learning and AI are intrinsically
related to causality, and explains how the field is beginning to
understand them.

bib.title: Causality for Machine Learning

bib.abstract:
Our ability to make logical inferences is considered as one of
the cornerstones of human intelligence, fuelling investigations
of reasoning abilities in non-human animals. Yet, the evidence to
date is equivocal, with apes as the prime candidates to possess
these skills. For instance, in a two-choice task, apes can
identify the location of hidden food if it is indicated by a
rattling noise caused by the shaking of a baited container. More
importantly, they also use the absence of noise during the
shaking of the empty container to infer that this container is
not baited. However, since the inaugural report of apes solving
this task, to the best of our knowledge, no comparable evidence
could be found in any other tested species such as monkeys and
dogs. Here, we report the first successful and instantaneous
solution of the shaking task through logical inference by a
non-ape species, the African grey parrot. Surprisingly, the
performance of the birds was sensitive to the shaking movement:
they were successful with containers shaken horizontally, but not
with vertical shaking resembling parrot head-bobbing. Thus, grey
parrots seem to possess ape-like cross-modal reasoning skills,
but their reliance on these abilities is influenced by low-level
interferences.
